Title: Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/strengthening-online-child-safety

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/strengthening-online-child-safety/

Markdown Content:
Today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our [Child Safety Blueprint](https://openai.com/index/introducing-child-safety-blueprint/) and our [ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse](https://openai.com/index/combating-online-child-sexual-exploitation-abuse/). For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

It is [well⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.esafety.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-02/Designing-for-Safety_Preventing-child-sexual-exploitation-and-abuse-online_CSEA-toolkit.pdf)[established⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/programs/lantern/) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

## Helping more organizations detect abusive material

We’re building on our [current protections](https://openai.com/index/combating-online-child-sexual-exploitation-abuse/) with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the [National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.missingkids.org/), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the [Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/) and [ROOST⁠(opens in a new window)](https://roost.tools/) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as [Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window)](https://safer.io/) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's [Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/programs/lantern/), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

“_Technology has an essential role to play in helping identify child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and, ultimately, the children who may be depicted in it. This new classifier gives more organizations access to tools that can help detect previously unidentified CSAM, strengthen reporting and provide critical information to those working to identify and protect victims. We’re grateful for OpenAI's investment to develop technology that strengthens the broader child safety ecosystem._”

**—John Shehan, Senior Vice President,**[**National Center for Missing & Exploited Children**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.missingkids.org/home)

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

### Results

Early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:

*   The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag **48%** fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

*   Images flagged by the new classifier were about **twice as likely** to contain abuse.

Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In [**fal**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://fal.ai/)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed **72%** of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. [**invideo AI**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://invideo.io/)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In [**SafetyKit**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.safetykit.com/)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected **90%** of cases.

“_Child safety tools need to recognize abuse across different types of content. In our testing, OpenAI’s classifier is the best we’ve seen, catching unknown CSAM that hash matching misses, including strong performance on drawings and animations, with false positives below 1% on legal adult content. These encouraging results point to broader protection against harmful content while limiting disruption for legitimate users._”

**—Samuel Wang, Member of Technical Staff,**[**SafetyKit**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.safetykit.com/)

More information about the classifier is available in the [CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/csam-image-classifier). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through [our intake form⁠](https://openai.com/form/csam-classifier-intake/). We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

## Interrupting harmful behavior and pointing people toward help

We already [prohibit CSAM](https://openai.com/index/combating-online-child-sexual-exploitation-abuse/), train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including [Protect Children⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.suojellaanlapsia.fi/en), the[Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.lucyfaithfull.org.uk/), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who [independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.utas.edu.au/about/news-and-stories/articles/2024/pioneering-chatbot-reduces-searches-for-illegal-sexual-images-of-children) of deterrent messages.

“_OpenAI has deployed a best-practice example in ChatGPT of how a platform can deter and disrupt harmful online behaviours. OpenAI has engaged multiple external experts who have previously designed and evaluated warning messages, built the intervention with them through evidence-based co-design, and aims to redirect users to local support options in as many jurisdictions as possible. This has given the warnings the best chance of steering users away from harm and towards support._”

**—Joel Scanlan, Associate Professor,**[**CSAM Deterrence Centre**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.csamdeterrence.com/our-team/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## Practical support for developers

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published [CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/csam-guidance) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the [Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/), [Thorn⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.thorn.org/), [NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.missingkids.org/home), and the [Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.iwf.org.uk/), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

The guidance provides clear rules, ways for users to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier, [Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/moderation), [ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window)](https://roost.tools/coop/), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as [Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window)](https://safer.io/).

Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the [Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/resources/responding-to-child-sexual-abuse-disclosures-in-ai-systems/), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

## Supporting child-safety law enforcement units

Protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve [discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a new window)](https://forum.openai.com/public/videos/event-replay-using-ai-to-protect-children-online-in-conversation-with-thorn-2026-02-11), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

We’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with new tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Title: Our first phase of embedded assessments

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/

Markdown Content:
We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our [safety cases](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/). They build on our [priorities and principles for third party assessments](https://openai.com/index/priorities-principles-third-party-assessments/) and years of work with [third party evaluators](https://openai.com/index/strengthening-safety-with-external-testing/), including a recent pilot assessment of [our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/) with deep internal access and an investigation of [the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

## Our pilot embedded assessors

### Apollo Research

In this pilot assessment, [Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

1.   Training did not incentivize subversion.

2.   Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

3.   Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

4.   Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

### Goodfire

[Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.goodfire.com/) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

### METR

We intend to conduct two assessments with [METR⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/), focused on model alignment and monitoring:

*   **Alignment assessment:** For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.[1](https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/#citation-bottom-1)

*   **Monitor assessment:** We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise[2](https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/#citation-bottom-2). We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another [monitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-14-control-assessment-proposal/) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

### Transluce

[Transluce⁠(opens in a new window)](https://transluce.org/) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

## Protocols for embedded assessments

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

### Scoping and iteration

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

### A secure, on-site environment

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum[3](https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/#citation-bottom-3) the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

### Oversight and dispute resolution

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

### Employee discussions and attestation

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

### Conflict disclosures & cool off periods

Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests[4](https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/#citation-bottom-4), and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods[5](https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/#citation-bottom-5) also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

### Publication and responsible disclosure periods

Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

## Looking ahead

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.

Title: Broadening access to AI for scientists

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/expanding-chatgpt-for-academic-researchers

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/expanding-chatgpt-for-academic-researchers/

Markdown Content:
We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

The program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for new drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing [_Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT_](https://openai.com/index/science-at-the-frontier/), new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

The program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot launched in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, we [contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/) to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

*   Through [ChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a new window)](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9377311-chatgpt-edu-at-openai), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

*   For researchers working in biology, [GPT‑Rosalind⁠](https://openai.com/rosalind/) brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The [Rosalind Academic Plan⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-the-rosalind-academic-plan/) helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Title: Science at the Frontier: How scientists use ChatGPT

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/science-at-the-frontier

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/science-at-the-frontier/

Markdown Content:
Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

Scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

## AI is part of scientists’ daily work

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

For each scientist, we calculated the share of their scientific messages in each activity, then averaged those shares, giving every scientist equal weight. Percentages are rounded; other research activities accounted for less than 1%.

## 68% of scientists used ChatGPT to develop research ideas

We looked at how scientists used ChatGPT for ideation. The figures below describe their messages about research ideas.

Led by scientist

35%

of the time, scientists brought a specific question for ChatGPT to work with.

Developed together

36%

of the time, scientists brought an idea and asked ChatGPT to refine it.

Suggested by ChatGPT

23%

of the time, scientists asked ChatGPT to suggest a research question.

Other

6%

The message could not be categorized into one of the other activities.

## 98% of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed up discovery in their field.

We asked scientists across different fields to imagine a discovery that would take 10 years without AI and estimate how long it would take with AI.

250 respondents answered this question. Respondents could select multiple fields, so field groups overlap. Percentages are rounded and may not total 100%.

## Scientists stay involved even after delegating tasks to ChatGPT

We measured how often scientists followed up to clarify, check, or revise ChatGPT’s responses across different research activities.

Average percentage of each scientist’s requests that led to a follow-up.

## How could AI further scientific progress?

We asked scientists who expected faster discovery to explain why. Three reasons stood out in their answers.

52%

Get research done faster

23%

Find more promising research questions

14%

Pursue a wider range of questions

11%

Other

Scientists could give multiple reasons. Percentages show the share of all 367 reasons identified in 224 written responses.

## Looking ahead

Scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

Understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding [ChatGPT for Academic Researchers⁠](https://openai.com/index/expanding-chatgpt-for-academic-researchers/), with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

“Tools like ChatGPT are helping us accelerate scientific discovery. It’s really a playground for a scientist like myself.”

César de la Fuente

## About the research

We analyzed 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists on the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers plan from August 20 to September 22, 2026.

The survey ran from September 30 to October 7, with 251 scientists’ responses presented in our analysis. The number of answers varies by question.

Title: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/advancing-computer-use-for-healthcare-teams

Markdown Content:
Healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care. When a clinician recommends an MRI, for example, the information an insurer needs may be in a patient’s medical record, but a team member still needs to retrieve it and enter it into a separate portal to complete an authorization request.

Computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing, and moving between applications. In healthcare, this enables AI to help with repetitive workflows in the software teams already use.

Today, we’re sharing new results measuring model performance, safety, and cost in clinical and administrative workflows. We’re also sharing the ways we’re working with leading healthcare organizations like Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health to advance and apply computer use, across authorization requests, referrals, discharge planning, and outreach between visits.

Healthcare teams, developers, and individual clinicians can access these capabilities today through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows, configure approvals and agent access, and record audit logs for secure deployments.

To show how a computer-use agent can help a clinician and an authorization specialist work on the same MRI request, we built a demo using synthetic patient data. A patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. A computer-use agent reviews the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records, and prior imaging in the EHR. It drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review. The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

OpenAI computer-use demonstration for healthcare teams

## Evaluating helpfulness, safety, and cost

We evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders, and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions, or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm. Overall, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated safe. Physicians rated helpfulness on a five-point scale, selecting “very helpful” or “extremely helpful” in 93% of 646 assessments.

### Examples of EHR Inbox work

#### Administrative workflow performance and cost

We also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals, and medical equipment orders. On[HealthAdminBench⁠(opens in a new window)](https://som-shahlab.github.io/health-admin-bench-website/), an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers measuring performance on common administrative workflows, GPT‑6 Astra earned 94.3% of available rubric points, while GPT‑6 Luna earned 91.8%, despite costing 98% less at 8.5 cents per task. Both models were evaluated at maximum reasoning effort. These results show progress toward capable, affordable agents for high-volume administrative workflows.

## Developing computer use with healthcare organizations

Our partners build software used in hundreds of health systems, coordinate care for members globally, and deliver care to hundreds of millions of patients. The following examples showcase how organizations are developing, piloting, and deploying computer-use applications to save time, solve critical problems, and improve patient care.

### CVS Health: Completing administrative work across clinical systems

CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals, and supporting specialist consults. The agents navigate existing applications to complete steps that APIs do not fully support.

In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend. Another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day, helping team members focus on work that needs their expertise. CVS Health uses validation checks and human oversight, with screenshots and action records to verify actions and application state. CVS Health is open sourcing its [Agent Kit⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/cvs-health/cua-agent-kit), built with OpenAI’s Agents SDK, which packages this approach as a repeatable process for broader use.

Data remains within the CVS Health enterprise-controlled infrastructure, governed by their enterprise AI Governance team and established responsible AI policies. Production data is not used to train foundation models.

### Abridge: Coordination across systems for every moment of care

Abridge is developing computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care plans across use cases and applications they use daily, including those without APIs. Their planned inpatient use case builds on the clinical conversation, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps.

For example, a clinician can ask the Abridge Assistant to help resolve a patient’s discharge barriers. Agents can work concurrently on medication access and home-health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages. The clinician stays focused on the patient and is brought in for decisions requiring clinical judgment.

Abridge computer-use demonstration for healthcare teams

### Cigna: Preparing care managers for member outreach

As part of The Cigna Group’s broader collaboration with OpenAI, Cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s frontier models alongside its own clinical expertise to bring together relevant information across systems and give care teams more complete context about each member’s needs and experience. That can include information about benefits and coverage, providers, appointments and prior interactions, helping care teams better support members around care plans established by their treating providers.

Previously, Cigna Healthcare case managers had to navigate more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather this context. Computer use can now help navigate these systems and bring relevant information together in seconds, reducing the time spent searching for information – ultimately giving case managers more time to support members.

### Ambience: Making computer use governable in healthcare

Computer use lets agents complete tasks in EHRs and payer portals that APIs don’t reach. In healthcare, that capability is only usable if every action is controlled and auditable. Ambience built additional controls to support that oversight.

In this demonstration, Ambience uses evidence from the patient’s chart to prepare a prior-authorization request on an insurer’s website. When the record is ambiguous, the agent stops and asks the clinician, then waits for approval before submitting. Health systems set which actions the agent can take, can pause it at any point, and get a step-by-step log for audit.

Ambience computer-use demonstration for healthcare teams

Healthcare startups are helping turn advances in computer use into new ways to support care teams. These five companies are combining AI agents with healthcare expertise to help teams navigate systems, coordinate next steps, and move care forward.

**Assort** | Closing the referral loop where the API can’t

#### Problem

Scheduling a visit doesn’t complete the referral workflow. Assort can attach a referral to the patient’s chart through Athena’s API, but closing it out requires a separate step in the EHR interface.

#### What they built

With computer use in Codex, Assort’s agent completes that step directly in Athena, extending the workflow past the limits of its existing API integration. The agent selects the referring provider, enters the referral details, and marks the referral “visit scheduled.”

#### Result

The referral reflected the scheduled appointment and dropped off the staff follow-up list.

## Patient data security and agent controls

Computer-use agents in healthcare require evaluating clinical safety, protecting patient information, and setting clear limits on what agents can do without human review.

ChatGPT for Healthcare provides role-based access controls and audit logs to support oversight. Organizations can build additional review and approval steps into their workflows and configure the applications and environments agents use to limit access to the records and actions needed for each task. Organization data is not used to train OpenAI foundation models.

To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI and the required security and retention settings.

## Get started with computer use agents

Computer-use agents for healthcare are available today in ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians, and the OpenAI API. Here’s how healthcare organizations, clinicians, and developers can get started.

*   **Healthcare organizations:**[Contact our sales team⁠](https://openai.com/contact-sales/) to discuss using AI in your clinical and administrative workflows. Existing customers can ask their workspace administrator to enable computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex.

*   **Individual clinicians:** U.S. clinicians can [sign up for a free ChatGPT for Clinicians account today⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/plans/clinicians/?openaicom-did=c11db7b5-e54e-4131-b4cf-9f45126b70c1&openaicom_referred=true) and experience computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex.

*   **Developers:** Build healthcare applications with the[OpenAI API⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/quickstart), and explore our[computer use guide⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-computer-use) to build agents that work across existing software.

We hope these advances enable healthcare teams to spend less time moving information through systems and more time caring for patients.

# NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab

November 16, 2026 by[Allen Bourgoyne](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/allenbourgoyne/ "Posts by Allen Bourgoyne")

 Share

Share This Article

At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers.

The kit is a four-node cluster of [NVIDIA DGX Spark systems](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/), each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks.

## **A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk**

The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work.

It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up.

At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1.

With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises.

The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems.

The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures.

Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for [Nemotron 3.5 Super VL](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-introduces-nemotron-for-science-to-accelerate-discoveries-with-agents) help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control.

## **What Researchers Can Do With It**

The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers.

Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions.

Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag.

Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter.

*   [Kvantify](https://www.kvantify.com/blog/nvidia-dgx-spark) is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations.
*   [CYRAN AI](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/case-studies/cyran-iit-delhi/), an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis.
*   [OpenFold](https://openfold.io/blog-finetuning-openfold3.html) shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery.
*   The [Rubin Lab at IGI](https://www.therubinlab.org/research) at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark.
*   The [Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley](https://hartwig.cchem.berkeley.edu/publications/?topic=10) is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back.

## **Where to Find the Kit**

The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through [NVIDIA Marketplace](https://marketplace.nvidia.com/en-us/enterprise/personal-ai-supercomputers/?manufacturer=NVIDIA&superchip=GB10&page=1&limit=15).

Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion.

An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems.

Title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/slurm-quantum-computing-supercomputing/

Published Time: 2026-11-16T16:00:47+00:00

Markdown Content:
Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors.

Many of these centers use [Slurm](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/slurm/) to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction.

In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware.

The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces.

## **Beating the Bottleneck**

Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions.

For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need.

Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month.

## **Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform**

The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform:

**CUDA-Q QEC** allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new [decoder server](https://nvidia.github.io/cuda-quantum/blogs/blog/2026/11/16/cudaq-qec-decoding-server/). A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard.

**CUDA-Q** gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months.

**CUDA-Q Algorithms**provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications

**CUDA-Q Pulse** gives quantum hardware builders a layer for [shaping the ‘pulses’](https://nvidia.github.io/cuda-quantum/blogs/blog/2026/11/16/introducing-cudaq-pulse/) needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation.

The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink.

At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built.

_Learn more about_[_NVIDIA quantum computing technologies_](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/quantum-computing/)_._

Title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/mlperf-training-endpoints-vera-rubin/

Published Time: 2026-11-16T16:00:25+00:00

Markdown Content:
In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference.

NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power.

These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s [CUDA-powered software stack](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/inference-software-lowest-token-cost/), so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time.

AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s [SC26 conference highlights](https://blogs.nvidia.com/sc26-news/), advancing scientific research.

Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster.

MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy.

The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation.

MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0116 , 6.1-0030, 6.1-0135, 6.1-0020, 6.1-0049, 6.1-0123, 6.1-0138, 6.1-0073, 6.1-0124, 6.1-0129 and 6.1-0038. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information.

NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four.

NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems.

Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times.

## **NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints**

An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task.

Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates.

MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks.

For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed.

MLPerf® Endpoints v1.0, Kimi K3, Standardized division, Available category, published November 9, 2026. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, 32 accelerators, result 1.0.1.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1p, run 9: concurrency = 1,024 queries, TTFT P90 = 4,673.9 ms, system TPS= 41,414.2 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 50.4 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 100.89 kW. NVIDIA GB300 NVL72, 48 accelerators, result1.0.0.kimi-k3.agentic_combined.1, run 6: concurrency = 48 queries, TTFT P90 = 2,305.1 ms, system TPS= 2,210.4 tokens/sec, E2E average interactivity = 56.2 tokens/sec per user, operating power = 60 kW. Comparison based on throughput per kilowatt at a shared minimum E2E average interactivity of 50 tokens/sec per user. Retrieved from endpoints.mlcommons.org on November 9, 2026. GB300 results verified by MLCommons Association. For the provisional Vera Rubin results: pending MLCommons Association verification, results are subject to change pending peer review. The MLPerf name and logo are registered and unregistered trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information.

Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster.

## **Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads**

NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure, Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus, Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE, Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida.

Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance.

The lead extends beyond MLPerf.

Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week.

_Dive deeper into the results in the [MLPerf Training](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-vera-rubin-nvl72-achieves-up-to-2x-blackwell-ultra-performance-in-mlperf-training-v6-1/) and_[_MLPerf Endpoints_](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-vera-rubin-nvl72-leads-agentic-inference-performance-on-mlperf-endpoints-v1-0/)_technical blogs._

# NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery

November 16, 2026 by[Kibibi Moseley](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/kibibimoseley/ "Posts by Kibibi Moseley")

Share This Article

With expanded [NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology.

The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems.

The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.

## **Bringing Black Holes Into Focus**

Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process.

With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the [cuPhoton Toolkit](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/high-performance-computing/ai-for-science/cuphoton/), black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes.

By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time.

The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact [NVIDIA DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/) system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull.

## **Steering Fusion Simulations**

Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results.

Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge.

The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/)-powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design.

## **Exploring Potential Medicines**

Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research, accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions.

NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER, NAMD, GROMACS, LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows.

Cadence, Fathom Therapeutics, Topos Bio, Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery.

## **Accelerating Materials Research**

Daviator, a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to [NVIDIA ALCHEMI](http://developer.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-x-libraries/alchemi) — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs.

At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.

The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments.

## **Revealing Biology at Scale**

The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs.

Codeveloped with scverse, the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, [Therna Biosciences](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/therna-biosciences-releases-chronos-the-data-engine-behind-its-ai-rna-biologist-302878554.html?tc=eml_cleartime) processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. # CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing

 Over two decades, CUDA, the platform that turned GPUs into the engine of modern science, has advanced Nobel Prize-winning research and more.

November 16, 2026 by[Brett Murray](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/bmurray/ "Posts by Brett Murray")

 Share

Share This Article

This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of [CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda) by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.

CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today.

At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.

## **From SC06 to SC26**

NVIDIA [announced CUDA in November 2006](https://web.archive.org/web/20220706095459/https://www.clustermonkey.net/Conference-Reports/sc06-jeffs-blog-day-1-sunday/Print.html) and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.

In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance [Nobel Prize-winning AI research](https://www.kva.se/en/news/the-nobel-prize-in-chemistry-2024/), accelerate [scientific applications on supercomputers](https://docs.nersc.gov/performance/readiness/) and support [visual effects in Oscar-winning films](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-quadro-powers-all-five-academy-award-nominees-for-best-visual-effects).

Today, [more than 11 million developers](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/gtc-2026-news/#cuda) build on CUDA across the computing stack.

## **Honoring the Architects of Progress**

Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:

At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through [Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/academia/whitepapers/Achievement2014_UIUC.pdf), tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on [Blue Waters](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Highlights/?highlight=2013-06&section=2013), one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.

In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to [train AlexNet](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf) on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system [won the 2012 ImageNet competition](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf), helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning.

That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s [publicly released AlphaFold 2 software](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold)[uses CUDA for GPU execution](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile).

These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.

# NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics

 A record leap in CUDA cores with accelerated data movement shorten time to results for science and engineering workloads.

November 16, 2026 by[Dan Ernst](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/dernst/ "Posts by Dan Ernst")

 Share

Share This Article

Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.

As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.

The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation [NVIDIA NVLink](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/nvlink/) interconnect technology.

Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

## **Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery**

Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.

To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.

That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.

These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.

[NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes.

And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.

_Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028._

Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup

The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when

, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident.
Other incidents were disclosed that day, too.
The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.
Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include
Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin
, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.
